To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
EPHA2 is a ligand-independent driver of the melanoma metastasis program and that EPHA2 activation is a mechanism by which targeted therapy induces metastasis in melanoma.
EPHA2 is a novel ligand-independent signaling molecule in human melanoma cells and EPHA2 signaling promotes a melanoma metastatic phenotype in vitro and in vivo.
EPHA2 signaling in the absence of its cognate ligand, ephrinA1, is sufficient to induce a melanoma metastatic phenotype.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of novel molecular pathways involved in the development of acquired resistance to targeted therapies in metastatic melanoma.
the development of a novel targeted therapy for the treatment of melanoma.

the development of novel, small-molecule inhibitors of EPHA2 kinase that are effective against melanoma and other EPH receptor-dependent cancers, and with the identification of the mechanisms by which EPHA2 signaling promotes melanoma metastasis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the EPHA2 signaling pathway is an important regulator of the metastatic process in melanoma and that EPHA2 signaling is an attractive therapeutic target for metastatic disease.
the ligand-independent activation of EPHA2 is an early and crucial step in melanoma progression and metastasis.
EPHA2 ligand-independent signaling drives the adoption and maintenance of the targeted therapy-mediated melanoma phenotype.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
EPHA2 is an oncogene and a therapeutic target in melanoma, and that the EPHA2 oncogene is activated through ligand-independent mechanisms in melanoma cells.
we have identified a novel mechanism for the adoption of a metastatic phenotype in melanoma, and that this mechanism is dependent upon the activation of EPHA2 by ligand-independent mechanisms.
the adoption of a metastatic phenotype in melanoma cells is dependent on the EPHA2 receptor tyrosine kinase.

we have shown that a ligand-independent form of EPHA2 can drive a metastatic phenotype in melanoma.
